domain_focus: AI/ML, LLM Evaluations, Decision Models & Reinforcement Learning

user_context.prompt: I am an ML systems engineer building a low-latency LLM serving engine. Teach me how Self-Attention memory bottlenecks work and how KV Caching, Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and PagedAttention solve them.
user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: Memory bandwidth bottlenecks in autoregressive decoding, KV cache sizing math, Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) vs Multi-Head Attention (MHA), and PagedAttention block management.

candidate_course.title: Transformer Inference Mechanics: From KV Cache Math to PagedAttention
candidate_course.description: A deep technical course on memory-bound autoregressive LLM decoding, KV cache memory footprint calculations, architectural head sharing via GQA, and virtual memory block management with PagedAttention.
candidate_course.target_audience: Advanced ML systems engineers optimizing LLM serving throughput and latency.

modules.title: Prefill vs. Decode: Arithmetic Intensity and the Memory Wall
modules.learning_objective: Distinguish compute-bound prefill from memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive decoding and calculate exact KV cache byte footprints per token.
modules.summary: Covers prefill matrix-matrix operations vs decode matrix-vector operations, roofline model arithmetic intensity, and deriving the formula 2 * layers * n_kv_heads * d_head * precision_bytes * seq_len.
sample_question_prompts: Calculate the exact KV cache footprint in GB for a 70B model with 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, FP16 precision, batch size 16, and sequence length 4096.
Why does increasing batch size during the decode phase improve GPU compute utilization up to the roofline knee point?

modules.title: Multi-Head (MHA), Multi-Query (MQA), and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
modules.learning_objective: Analyze how sharing Key and Value projections across query head groups reduces KV cache memory bandwidth overhead while preserving model quality.
modules.summary: Compares standard MHA, extreme MQA (1 KV head), and GQA (g groups of query heads sharing KV heads), examining tensor shapes and broadcast mechanics during attention score computation.
sample_question_prompts: In Grouped-Query Attention with 32 query heads and 4 KV heads, how are Key tensors broadcast or repeated to compute QK^T?
What is the primary trade-off between Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) when uptraining an existing MHA checkpoint?

modules.title: Eliminating Fragmentation with PagedAttention
modules.learning_objective: Explain internal and external memory fragmentation in contiguous KV cache allocation and how PagedAttention maps logical token blocks to non-contiguous physical GPU memory blocks.
modules.summary: Examines why pre-allocating max_seq_len contiguous buffers wastes 60-80% of VRAM, how block tables map logical blocks to fixed-size physical KV blocks, and copy-on-write mechanics for parallel sampling and beam search.
sample_question_prompts: How does PagedAttention handle shared prefixes across multiple candidate completions using reference counts and copy-on-write?
Which type of memory fragmentation occurs when a request reserves 2048 token slots contiguously in VRAM but terminates after generating 150 tokens?

modules.title: Continuous Batching & FlashDecoding Kernel Mechanics
modules.learning_objective: Combine iteration-level scheduling with parallelized sequence-dimension reduction in FlashDecoding to maximize tokens/sec under SLA latency bounds.
modules.summary: Covers iteration-level batching (replacing completed sequences immediately without waiting for stragglers) and splitting KV cache across the sequence length dimension with online softmax rescaling.
sample_question_prompts: Why does standard FlashAttention underutilize streaming multiprocessors (SMs) during small-batch autoregressive decoding, and how does FlashDecoding fix this?
Explain how online softmax combines partial attention outputs across split KV sequence chunks using log-sum-exp rescaling factors.

expected.rationale: The course directly targets the advanced systems engineer's goal, progressing logically from roofline arithmetic intensity and exact KV cache byte math to GQA head sharing, PagedAttention virtual block tables, and continuous batching. Every module integrates both multiple-choice and rigorous short-answer assessments.

course_quality_evals.domain: Post-Training Alignment: RLHF & Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

user_context.prompt: I know supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and now I want to understand the math and engineering behind RLHF (Bradley-Terry reward modeling + PPO) and how DPO eliminates the separate reward model.
user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: Bradley-Terry preference modeling, PPO objective with KL penalty in RLHF, the closed-form derivation of DPO via the optimal policy-reward mapping, and practical failure modes like reward hacking and likelihood displacement.

candidate_course.title: Mathematical & Practical Foundations of LLM Preference Alignment: RLHF to DPO
candidate_course.description: A rigorous progression from pairwise preference modeling and four-model PPO loops to Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and alignment pathology debugging.
candidate_course.target_audience: ML researchers and engineers experienced with SFT who want deep mathematical and practical mastery of preference alignment.

modules.title: Pairwise Human Preferences & The Bradley-Terry Reward Model
modules.learning_objective: Derive the cross-entropy loss for training a reward model on pairwise comparisons (y_w > y_l | x) under the Bradley-Terry probabilistic framework.
modules.summary: Formulates preference probability P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)), explains why reward scores are shift-invariant per prompt, and covers sequence-level scalar head architecture.
sample_question_prompts: Why is adding a prompt-dependent function f(x) to a reward model r(x, y) neutral under the Bradley-Terry preference probability?
Which token position's hidden state is typically projected to produce the scalar reward in a causal decoder-only reward model?

modules.title: KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning & The Four-Model PPO Loop
modules.learning_objective: Formulate the KL-constrained reward maximization objective and explain the roles of the Actor, Reference Policy, Critic, and Reward Model in RLHF.
modules.summary: Covers the objective E[r(x,y) - beta * D_KL(pi_theta || pi_ref)], why omitting the KL penalty causes mode collapse and reward over-optimization, and the memory pressure of hosting four models in VRAM.
sample_question_prompts: What happens to policy entropy and reward model scores if beta (the KL penalty coefficient) is set too close to zero during PPO?
Explain the distinct functions of the frozen reference policy (pi_ref) and the trainable value critic (V_phi) during a PPO update step.

modules.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): Reparameterizing the Optimal Policy
modules.learning_objective: Derive the DPO loss by expressing the ground-truth reward in terms of the optimal policy pi* and reference policy pi_ref, eliminating the explicit reward model and RL sampling loop.
modules.summary: Shows r(x,y) = beta * log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta * log Z(x), cancels the intractable partition function Z(x) inside the Bradley-Terry difference, and analyzes the per-example gradient weighting term.
sample_question_prompts: How does the partition function Z(x) disappear when substituting the analytical optimal policy rearrangement into the Bradley-Terry preference model?
Interpret the gradient weight factor sigma(beta * log(pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) - beta * log(pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x))) in the DPO loss gradient.

modules.title: Alignment Pathologies: Length Bias, Likelihood Displacement & Off-Policy Drift
modules.learning_objective: Diagnose practical pathologies in DPO and RLHF including verbosity bias, simultaneous decrease in log-probability of both chosen and rejected responses, and distribution shift.
modules.summary: Compares online on-policy sampling in PPO vs offline static preference datasets in DPO, length-normalized variants (SimPO/IPO), and monitoring implicit reward margins during training.
sample_question_prompts: Why can DPO decrease the absolute log-likelihood of the winning response y_w while still increasing the implicit reward margin between y_w and y_l?
How does length bias emerge in unnormalized sequence-level log-probability ratios, and how do length-controlled objectives mitigate it?

expected.rationale: Excellently structured progression from Bradley-Terry reward modeling to KL-regularized PPO, followed by the exact mathematical bridge to DPO (partition function cancellation and implicit reward gradients) and real-world pathologies.

course_quality_evals.domain: JEV/Clef Decision Classifiers, Calibration & LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: LLM-as-a-Judge biases (position, verbosity, self-preference), JEV/Clef decision threshold calibration (ECE, Brier score, temperature scaling), and Rogan-Gladen correction for estimating true pass rates with an imperfect classifier.

candidate_course.title: Calibrated Decision Classifiers & Robust LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
candidate_course.description: Learn how to design, debias, and statistically calibrate LLM verifiers and JEV-style Clef decision models for high-stakes adaptive grading and evaluation pipelines.
candidate_course.target_audience: AI engineers building automated evaluation pipelines and adaptive decision systems.

modules.title: Anatomy of LLM-as-a-Judge Biases and Rubric Decomposition
modules.learning_objective: Identify and mitigate position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias using position-swapped pairwise evaluation and atomic binary/pointwise rubrics.
modules.summary: Demonstrates why 1-10 holistic Likert scales yield low inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa) and how decomposing rubrics into explicit boolean criteria plus position swapping stabilizes judge outputs.
sample_question_prompts: When running pairwise comparisons between Model A and Model B, how do you detect and handle inconsistent judgments after swapping the order of responses?
Why do decomposed binary rubric checklists outperform unconstrained 1-to-10 integer scoring prompts in LLM evaluators?

modules.title: JEV-Style Clef Decision Models: Conditioning on Goal & Learner State
modules.learning_objective: Design a contextual decision classifier that evaluates student responses relative to user-specific learning goals, rigor preferences, and historical misconceptions.
modules.summary: Explains why correctness in adaptive learning is conditioned on (question, reference_rubric, user_goal, rigor_preference) rather than static string matching, and how Clef classifiers map token logprobs to structured pedagogical actions.
sample_question_prompts: Give an example where identical student answers should receive different `is_right` decisions from a Clef classifier based solely on the user's `rigor_preference`.
How do you extract normalized decision probabilities from first-token logits of a fine-tuned classifier head?

modules.title: Probability Calibration, Expected Calibration Error (ECE) & Temperature Scaling
modules.learning_objective: Compute Brier Score and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on a held-out gold human set and apply post-hoc Temperature Scaling or Platt Scaling to calibrate decision thresholds.
modules.summary: Covers reliability diagrams, why RLHF/instruction-tuned models are systematically overconfident (sharpened logit distributions), and fitting scalar temperature T > 1 on validation logits without changing argmax accuracy.
sample_question_prompts: Why does post-hoc single-parameter Temperature Scaling alter Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier Score while leaving top-1 classification accuracy unchanged?
Calculate the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) across two confidence bins given bin sample counts, mean predicted probabilities, and empirical accuracies.

modules.title: Estimating True System Performance with Imperfect Judges (Rogan-Gladen & CIs)
modules.learning_objective: Apply the Rogan-Gladen estimator and bootstrap confidence intervals to adjust raw judge pass rates using the judge's measured sensitivity (TPR) and specificity (TNR) on a gold audit set.
modules.summary: Derives p_hat = (q_raw + q_0 - 1) / (q_1 + q_0 - 1) where q_1 is sensitivity and q_0 is specificity, showing how uncorrected biases skew benchmark rankings.
sample_question_prompts: If an LLM judge has sensitivity TPR = 0.90 and specificity TNR = 0.80 on a human-labeled gold set, and predicts a raw pass rate of 0.62 on production traffic, what is the Rogan-Gladen bias-corrected true pass rate?
Why must uncertainty from both the finite gold calibration set and the test evaluation set be propagated when constructing confidence intervals?

expected.rationale: Directly addresses all three aspects of the user's request—judge biases, JEV/Clef conditional decision modeling with probability calibration (ECE, Brier, temperature scaling), and Rogan-Gladen statistical bias correction—at an appropriate intermediate-to-advanced engineering depth.

modules.learning_objective: Decide whether a product requirement calls for RAG, LoRA fine-tuning, or both based on data volatility, citation requirements, and output format constraints.

module_context.course_title: Transformer Inference Mechanics: From KV Cache Math to PagedAttention
module_context.module_title: Multi-Head (MHA), Multi-Query (MQA), and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
module_context.learning_objective: Calculate KV cache memory footprint reductions when transitioning from Multi-Head Attention to Grouped-Query Attention.

candidate_question.prompt: Consider a 32-layer Transformer with hidden dimension d_model = 4096, 32 query heads, head dimension d_head = 128, and FP16 (2 bytes per element) KV cache storage. If the architecture is converted from standard Multi-Head Attention (32 KV heads) to Grouped-Query Attention with 4 KV heads (GQA-4), how much KV cache memory is required to store a single sequence of 8,192 tokens?
options: 512 MB (reduced by 8x from 4,096 MB in MHA)
1,024 MB (reduced by 4x from 4,096 MB in MHA)
256 MB (reduced by 8x from 2,048 MB in MHA)
4,096 MB (GQA reduces parameter count in W_Q, not KV cache size)
candidate_question.correct_answer: 512 MB (reduced by 8x from 4,096 MB in MHA)
candidate_question.grading_notes: Formula: 2 (K and V) * 32 layers * 4 KV_heads * 128 d_head * 2 bytes (FP16) * 8192 tokens = 536,870,912 bytes = 512 MiB (or MB in binary megabytes). Distractor 2 forgets the 8x ratio; Distractor 3 forgets the factor of 2 for both K and V; Distractor 4 tests the misconception that GQA compresses query weights rather than KV cache.

expected.rationale: Clear, unambiguous quantitative question tailored to an advanced learner. Every distractor maps to a specific diagnostic error (forgetting the factor of 2 for K+V, miscalculating the head reduction ratio, or confusing KV cache compression with query weight compression).

question_quality_evals.domain: Post-Training Alignment: RLHF & Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

user_context.what_user_wants_to_learn: How the DPO loss gradient weights examples based on implicit reward margins and why reference policy log-ratios matter.
user_context.prior_feedback_summary: User mastered the Bradley-Terry reward formulation and is now analyzing the mechanics of the DPO loss gradient.

module_context.course_title: Mathematical & Practical Foundations of LLM Preference Alignment: RLHF to DPO
module_context.module_title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): Reparameterizing the Optimal Policy
module_context.learning_objective: Derive and interpret the gradient of the DPO loss with respect to policy parameters theta.

candidate_question.prompt: In the gradient of the DPO loss with respect to policy parameters theta, each preference pair (x, y_w, y_l) is weighted by the scalar term sigma(r_hat(x, y_l) - r_hat(x, y_w)), where r_hat(x, y) = beta * log(pi_theta(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x)). Explain what this weighting term does dynamically when the implicit reward model currently ranks the rejected response y_l higher than the winning response y_w, and why omitting the normalization by pi_ref(y|x) would cause policy degradation.
candidate_question.correct_answer: When the implicit reward model incorrectly assigns a higher score to the rejected response y_l than to the chosen response y_w (so r_hat(x, y_l) - r_hat(x, y_w) > 0), the sigmoid weight sigma(...) exceeds 0.5 and approaches 1, scaling up the gradient update for pairs where the policy's implicit ranking is most wrong. Conversely, when y_w is already strongly preferred over y_l, the weight approaches 0. Omitting pi_ref(y|x) removes the KL-divergence anchor to the reference policy, causing the model to degenerate by assigning high probability to out-of-distribution or repetitive sequences and collapsing linguistic coherence.
candidate_question.grading_notes: Must cover two key points: (1) the sigmoid term acts as an adaptive importance weight that upweights preference pairs where the policy currently prefers y_l over y_w (misordered implicit reward margin), and (2) dividing by pi_ref enforces the KL constraint to prevent policy collapse/degeneration.

expected.rationale: High-rigor short-answer question that directly probes the mathematical intuition of DPO's gradient weighting term and the role of the reference policy, with an explicit two-part grading rubric.

candidate_question.prompt: In standard LoRA (without 4-bit quantization), the pretrained weight matrix W_0 remains in 16-bit precision in GPU memory, yet total training VRAM drops drastically compared to full fine-tuning. candidate_question.correct_answer: (1) Freezing W_0 eliminates the need to store weight gradients and Adam/AdamW optimizer states (first and second momentum buffers, which normally consume 2x to 4x the memory of the FP16 weights themselves) for the billions of base parameters; gradients and optimizer states are only stored for the tiny trainable matrices A and B. (2) Initializing B=0 ensures the adapter output Delta W = B*A is exactly zero at step 0 so the model starts with the exact pretrained behavior of W_0. If both A and B were initialized to zero, the gradients with respect to both A and B would be zero (a saddle point), preventing any learning via gradient descent.

expected.rationale: Explicitly builds on the learner's prior misconception (`W_0` weight size vs optimizer state/gradient size) and asks a clear two-part conceptual short-answer question with a well-defined grading rubric.

question.prompt: Let q, k in R^{d_k} have independent components with mean 0 and variance 1. (1) Show why Var(q^T k) = d_k and why scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) prevents softmax Jacobian collapse. (2) Write the exact byte expression for the KV cache read per decode step for batch size B, sequence length S, layers L, KV heads H_kv, head dimension d_k, and 2-byte FP16 precision.
question.reference_answer: (1) Each product q_i k_i has E[q_i k_i] = E[q_i]E[k_i] = 0 and Var(q_i k_i) = E[q_i^2]E[k_i^2] = 1. Summing d_k independent terms gives Var(sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i) = d_k. Without dividing by sqrt(d_k), large d_k causes logits to grow as O(sqrt(d_k)), driving softmax outputs toward 0 or 1 where the Jacobian diag(p) - pp^T vanishes. (2) Bytes read per decode step = 2 * B * S * L * H_kv * d_k * 2 = 4 * B * S * L * H_kv * d_k bytes.
required_concepts_for_user_goal: Var(q_i k_i) = 1 summed over d_k independent components yields Var(q^T k) = d_k
scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) normalizes variance to 1 to prevent softmax saturation / vanishing Jacobian
exact KV cache bytes read = 2 (K and V) * B * S * L * H_kv * d_k * 2 bytes
question.grading_rubric: Requires both the formal variance derivation Var(q^T k) = d_k with softmax saturation explanation and the exact byte formula including the factor of 2 for K and V and 2 bytes for FP16.

user_submission.answer: 1) Since q_i and k_i are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, E[q_i k_i] = 0 and Var(q_i k_i) = E[q_i^2]E[k_i^2] = 1. Summing over d_k independent coordinates gives Var(q^T k) = d_k. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) scales the variance back to 1; otherwise for large d_k the logit magnitudes blow up, pushing softmax into saturation where p_i -> 1 or 0 and the gradient/Jacobian diag(p) - p p^T vanishes. 2) Per decode step, we read both K and V (factor of 2) across L layers, H_kv heads, d_k dimension, sequence length S, and batch B at 2 bytes per FP16 element: 2 * B * S * L * H_kv * d_k * 2 = 4 * B * S * L * H_kv * d_k bytes.

scaling by 1/sqrt(d_k) normalizes variance to 1 to prevent softmax saturation / vanishing Jacobian
exact KV cache bytes read = 2 (K and V) * B * S * L * H_kv * d_k * 2 bytes

module_context.learning_objective: Explain how LoRA adapters are merged into base weights for zero-latency single-tenant inference vs unmerged for multi-tenant serving.

question.prompt: After training a LoRA adapter (matrices A and B with scaling factor alpha/r) on a frozen base weight matrix W_0, how can you deploy the adapted model for a single dedicated model endpoint with zero additional inference latency compared to the original base model? Furthermore, what is the trade-off if you instead need to serve 50 different customer-specific LoRA adapters simultaneously on the same GPU?
question.reference_answer: For a single endpoint, you can offline merge the adapter directly into the base weights by computing W_merged = W_0 + (alpha / r) * B * A because matrix multiplication is linear; at inference time, only W_merged is executed with zero extra latency or parameters. However, if serving 50 customer adapters on one GPU, merging creates 50 full copies of the multi-gigabyte model in VRAM; instead, you keep one shared frozen W_0 in VRAM and dynamically compute the small low-rank branch (alpha/r)*B_i*(A_i*x) per request in batch (e.g., S-LoRA/Punica) at a slight compute overhead.
required_concepts_for_user_goal: linear weight merging W_merged = W_0 + (alpha/r) * B * A eliminates single-model inference latency overhead
multi-tenant trade-off: merging duplicates full model VRAM vs keeping shared W_0 and applying unmerged adapters dynamically per request
question.grading_rubric: Requires both: (1) explaining how W_0 + (alpha/r)*B*A merges weights for zero single-tenant latency, and (2) explaining the multi-tenant VRAM vs compute trade-off when serving 50 adapters.

user_submission.answer: Because the LoRA update is linear, you can just add the trained low-rank matrices directly into the base weights before deployment: W_new = W_0 + (alpha/r) * B * A. That way the matrix dimensions are identical to the original model and inference has zero extra latency.

user_profile.what_user_wants_to_learn: Diagnosing and eliminating position bias and verbosity bias in LLM-as-a-Judge pairwise evaluations.

module_context.course_title: Calibrated Decision Classifiers & Robust LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
module_context.module_title: Anatomy of LLM-as-a-Judge Biases and Rubric Decomposition
module_context.learning_objective: Implement position-swapped pairwise evaluation protocols to detect and neutralize position bias.

question.prompt: You are using an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare Candidate Response A and Candidate Response B, and you suspect the judge suffers from position bias (favoring whichever response appears first in the prompt). Describe the exact inference protocol used to detect and neutralize position bias for each evaluation pair, including how you score cases where the judge's verdict flips.
question.reference_answer: Run every pairwise comparison twice: once in order (A, B) and once with positions swapped as (B, A). A model only wins if the judge consistently selects that same underlying response in both orderings (e.g., picks Slot 1 in (A,B) and Slot 2 in (B,A)). If the judge picks Slot 1 in both calls (or Slot 2 in both calls), the judgment is position-biased/inconsistent and should be recorded as a tie (or routed to a tie-breaker/human audit).
required_concepts_for_user_goal: evaluate each pair twice with swapped positions (A,B) and (B,A)
require consistent winner across both orderings; treat position-dependent flips as ties/inconsistent
question.grading_rubric: Must mention running both (A,B) and (B,A) orderings and treating inconsistent/position-locked outcomes as ties (or routing for tie-breaking).

user_submission.answer: For every test prompt, call the judge twice: first passing (Response A, Response B) and second swapping their slots to (Response B, Response A). We only award a win to A or B if the judge picks the same actual response in both runs. If the judge just picks the first slot both times (picking A in run 1 and B in run 2), we flag it as position bias and score the pair as a tie.

matched_concepts: evaluate each pair twice with swapped positions (A,B) and (B,A)
require consistent winner across both orderings; treat position-dependent flips as ties/inconsistent
expected_decision.feedback_focus: Confirm the position-swapping protocol `(A,B)` + `(B,A)` and tie-handling rule for inconsistent judgments.
expected_decision.rationale: The student's response clearly and accurately describes both the position-swapped dual invocation and how inconsistent slot-locked verdicts are scored as ties.

user_profile.what_user_wants_to_learn: Why autoregressive LLM generation uses a KV cache and why the decode step is memory-bandwidth bound.

module_context.course_title: Transformer Inference Mechanics: From KV Cache Math to PagedAttention
module_context.module_title: Prefill vs. Decode: Arithmetic Intensity and the Memory Wall
module_context.learning_objective: Understand what values are cached in the KV cache and why Query vectors do not need to be cached across past tokens.

prior_misconceptions: Confuses causal attention dependencies at step t with needing past Query vectors Q_{1..t-1}.

question.prompt: During autoregressive decoding at token step t, why do we cache the Key (K) and Value (V) vectors for all previous tokens 1..t-1 in GPU memory, but we do NOT cache the Query (Q) vectors for previous tokens 1..t-1?
question.reference_answer: Under causal masking, the hidden states and outputs for tokens 1..t-1 have already been computed and never change (since past tokens cannot attend to future token t). To generate token t+1, we only need to compute the attention output for the newest token t, which requires multiplying the current token's query vector q_t against all past keys K_{1..t} and weighting all past values V_{1..t}. Past query vectors q_{1..t-1} are never used again.
required_concepts_for_user_goal: only current query q_t is needed at step t to attend over all past keys K_{1..t} and values V_{1..t}
causal masking means past tokens 1..t-1 do not attend to future tokens so their outputs are already finalized
question.grading_rubric: Must explain that generating the next token at step t only requires computing attention for the new query q_t against past K_{1..t} and V_{1..t}, whereas past queries q_{1..t-1} were only needed at their own earlier steps.

user_submission.answer: We don't cache Q because the Query matrix W_Q has zero trainable parameters and is deleted after prefill, whereas K and V are updated via gradient descent on every generated token.

missed_concepts: only current query q_t is needed at step t to attend over all past keys K_{1..t} and values V_{1..t}
causal masking means past tokens 1..t-1 do not attend to future tokens so their outputs are already finalized
expected_decision.detected_misconception: Confuses inference-time KV caching with gradient descent weight updates and falsely believes W_Q has no parameters or is deleted after prefill.
expected_decision.feedback_focus: Clarify that all projection matrices (`W_Q`, `W_K`, `W_V`) remain frozen during inference and `W_Q` projects the newest token `x_t` into `q_t` at every step; past `q_{1..t-1}` aren't cached simply because step `t` only computes `softmax(q_t K_{1..t}^T / sqrt(d_k)) V_{1..t}`.
expected_decision.rationale: This is the learner's 2nd attempt with low recent accuracy (0.45) and reveals a fundamental misconception about inference vs training and how `q_t` interacts with `K_{1..t}` and `V_{1..t}`. Stepping down to a scaffolded `ask_remedial_multiple_choice` is the appropriate pedagogical action.

user_profile.what_user_wants_to_learn: Diagnosing RAG evaluation failures using RAGAS/TruLens triad metrics (Context Recall, Faithfulness/Groundedness, Answer Relevance).

module_context.course_title: Evaluating & Debugging Production RAG Systems
module_context.module_title: The RAG Triad: Context Relevance/Recall, Groundedness (Faithfulness), and Answer Relevance
module_context.learning_objective: Isolate whether a bad RAG response stems from a retrieval failure or a generation hallucination using triad evaluation scores.

question.prompt: On a failing test query in your RAG benchmark, your evaluation pipeline reports: Context Recall = 0.96, Context Precision = 0.92, Faithfulness (Groundedness) = 0.21, and Answer Relevance = 0.88. Which component of your RAG pipeline is failing, and what is the most targeted fix?
options: The generator LLM is hallucinating claims not supported by the retrieved chunks despite the retriever fetching the right context; fix by tightening system prompt grounding constraints, lowering generation temperature, or fine-tuning/swapping the generator.
The vector database embedding model is failing to retrieve the relevant documents; fix by reducing chunk size and adding BM25 hybrid search.
The user query rewriter is stripping essential keywords before retrieval; fix by disabling query expansion.
The cross-encoder reranker is dropping the gold document chunk before it reaches the prompt; fix by increasing top-K from 5 to 20.
question.reference_answer: The generator LLM is hallucinating claims not supported by the retrieved chunks despite the retriever fetching the right context; fix by tightening system prompt grounding constraints, lowering generation temperature, or fine-tuning/swapping the generator.
required_concepts_for_user_goal: high Context Recall/Precision (0.96/0.92) proves retrieval succeeded
low Faithfulness/Groundedness (0.21) isolates the failure to ungrounded generator hallucination
question.grading_rubric: Option A is correct. Options B, C, and D misdiagnose the issue as a retrieval failure despite Context Recall = 0.96 and Context Precision = 0.92.

user_submission.answer: The vector database embedding model is failing to retrieve the relevant documents; fix by reducing chunk size and adding BM25 hybrid search.

missed_concepts: high Context Recall/Precision (0.96/0.92) proves retrieval succeeded
low Faithfulness/Groundedness (0.21) isolates the failure to ungrounded generator hallucination
expected_decision.detected_misconception: Confuses low Faithfulness (generator hallucinating beyond retrieved context) with low Context Recall (retriever failing to fetch relevant chunks).
expected_decision.feedback_focus: Contrast Context Recall (0.96 means the retriever already placed the needed facts into the prompt) with Faithfulness/Groundedness (0.21 means the generator fabricated claims unsupported by that retrieved context).
expected_decision.rationale: The student diagnosed a retrieval failure even though Context Recall (0.96) and Context Precision (0.92) are both near-perfect and only Faithfulness (0.21) is low. Re-explaining how the RAG Triad separates retrieval metrics from generation faithfulness directly addresses this confusion.
